title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6855 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: Gold traders see plenty of drama after US CPI but still no clear winner for now
body: It's been a back and forth kind of week for gold so far, with there being plenty of pushing and pulling in general. And we also got a little drama courtesy of the US CPI report yesterday, yet somehow we're still going around in circles - more or less. For all the excitement, we're just seemingly going back to where we started the week. Oh, what fun. Pfft. Anyway, the hotter-than-expected inflation numbers yesterday gave sellers a reason to pounce as both the monthly headline and core inflation readings came in above estimates. That saw Treasury yields surge higher alongside the dollar, putting gold under heavy pressure as markets ramped up bets on further Fed tightening. But despite the heavy selloff, gold managed to find support near $4,020 before bouncing back towards $4,060 today. And despite the recovery since last week, gold buyers still haven't exactly made much meaningful progress in establishing a firmer bullish footing. Looking at the hourly chart, buyers managed to somewhat defend the 200-hour moving average (blue line) in overnight trading but are now facing a familiar resistance hurdle in the form of the 100-hour moving average (red line) next. The latter sits around $4,088 currently and offers the first key near-term test for buyers in the latest bounce today. Beyond that, the $4,140-46 region has repeatedly capped upside attempts so far this month, making it the more important near-term resistance to break.

title: Germany October inflation slows, but winter energy risks keep ECB rate hike bets alive
body: Germany October final CPI +2.8% vs +2.8% y/y prelim Prior +3.3% Germany October final HICP +2.8% vs +2.8% y/y prelim Prior +3.3% The final report here pretty much confirms what we already seen with the preliminary report from earlier. The easing in price pressures in Europe's largest economy owed much to a slower increase in energy prices in October, as well as the introduction of temporary fuel tax cuts starting 1 October (scheduled to run through the end of the year). That being said, all measures of underlying inflation also fell with services and goods prices also dropping on the month. Destatis notes that: "The main reason for the continued high inflation rate remained the development of energy prices, even though the fuel discount, which was reintroduced at the beginning of October, likely dampened inflation somewhat." The more crucial estimate, that being core annual inflation, is reaffirmed at 2.1% in October - marking a drop from 2.4% in September. So, that will offer some comfort to the ECB that price pressures are not exactly surging all across the region towards the final quarter of the year. Having said that, do be reminded that we are approaching the start of the winter season. And combined with low gas storage levels, that is also likely to push up gas prices in the coming weeks. In turn, that could possibly translate into higher retail/consumer prices at the start of next year.

title: Heads up: US bond market closed for Veterans Day as stocks face a hot CPI hangover
body: Talk about picking an awkward time to take a day off, eh? Wall Street was left licking its wounds yesterday after the hotter-than-expected US inflation data sent Treasury yields surging and stocks tumbling. And just as traders are trying to make sense of the fallout, the bond market is going to be off on a holiday. A reminder and a quick heads up that today is Veterans Day in the US, meaning the bond market will be closed while stock markets will remain open as per usual. As such, that makes for a rather peculiar setup after yesterday's market reaction to the inflation numbers. Headline inflation came in at 0.4% m/m in October against the 0.3% expected, while core inflation rose by 0.3% m/m versus estimates of 0.2%. And that was enough to reignite concerns over the Fed potentially having to tighten policy more aggressively in December, especially after Fed governor Waller warned about perhaps needing to move by 50 bps on stronger price pressures than anticipated. The bond market reaction was jarring. 2-year Treasury yields jumped by roughly 18 bps to 4.74%, while 10-year yields climbed by around 12 bps to to settle at 5%. In turn, equities weren't too pleased with the S&P 500 falling 0.4% and the Nasdaq shedding 0.7%. But for a late recovery, the selloff in stocks would've been much worse. So, what does that mean for trading today?

title: Euro bears haven't been this aggressive since the Covid pandemic, but is the trade getting too crowded?
body: The euro certainly isn't winning any popularity contests these days. A fragile growth outlook alongside surging energy prices and growing fiscal concerns in France has left traders with little reason to cheer for the single currency. And judging by the latest CFTC positioning data, leveraged funds aren't just turning their backs on the euro as well. They're practically racing each other to bet against it. But when a consensus trade becomes too heavy and one-sided, there's always the risk that it can get a little too crowded for comfort. That is precisely what MUFG is warning about in highlighting that speculative short positions in the euro have now reached their highest level since the Covid pandemic in early 2020. The latest CFTC positioning data shows that leveraged funds are holding a net short position of 78,559 euro futures contracts as of 3 November. That is up sharply from just 28,156 contracts in mid-September. MUFG notes that: "The recent unfavourable combination of higher energy prices and government borrowing costs particularly in France has reinforced euro selling pressure. The release of the latest IMM positioning report at the end of last week revealed leveraged funds are heavily short the euro." As mentioned, the bearish sentiment on the single currency isn't all too surprising. Europe's energy vulnerability has returned to be a hot topic amid the US-Iran conflict, with higher oil prices threatening to make the ECB's inflation headache even worse.

title: Morgan Stanley's Wilson: correction in final phase, three reasons oil can fall into 2027
body: A major-bank strategist calling the correction's final phase gives dip buyers support, especially alongside the post-midterm seasonal record. Oil is the key link. If Brent and WTI keep falling on demand destruction and new non-Hormuz supply, that would ease inflation pressure and could temper Fed hike expectations, a significant shift from oil as the main inflation risk this year. The flip side is that any renewed escalation in the Middle East would quickly undercut his thesis. His target range near current levels suggests limited further downside in his view, but his warning against timing the bottom points to more volatility first. --- Wilson says the worst of the correction is nearly done, and the next tailwind for stocks could be the oil price that has troubled them all year.

title: CoreWeave stock jumps nearly 13% after earnings. Buy the rally or sell into resistance?
body: CoreWeave (NASDAQ: CRWV) surged approximately 12.6% in overnight trading following its November 10 earnings, but the advance was anything but straightforward. The stock initially rallied, nearly surrendered its gains, and then recovered dramatically. For traders deciding whether to buy, sell or wait, what happened between those moves may be more important than the final percentage gain. Why CoreWeave's earnings matter for the entire AI trade The results arrive at an unusually sensitive moment for AI investors. There's a growing debate about whether enormous spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure will produce adequate financial returns. Demand for computing power may be extraordinary, but investors increasingly want to know who will finance the expansion, at what cost, and when the investment will translate into sustainable profits. I'm keeping a close eye on the broader AI and data-centre trade this week, as structural constraints and massive capital flows are colliding to create serious volatility. On the supply side, we're about to see a major gauge of retail appetite with Anthropic allocating up to 20% of its massive $64 billion IPO directly to retail investors. Meanwhile, the physical limitations of scaling AI capacity are starting to hit balance sheets, highlighted by SoftBank swinging to a massive $7 billion Q2 loss following a brutal $3.7 billion hit on US data centre power equipment.
